issues: Type-I calibration, which is half of the claim, is barely tested. `R_NULL = 3` gives at most 3 null replications per run, so `type1` can only be 0, 1/3, 2/3 or 1, and it is not part of the primary metric. Inflated size from the deep kernel would not show up.

The power estimate is coarse. `R_ALT = 6` means power moves in steps of 1/6 ≈ 0.167 per run, which is far larger than the declared `min_effect: 0.05`. Many seeds are needed before an effect of that size can be resolved.

Both nuisances can be misspecified at the same time, so double robustness can fail. The propensity is clipped with `np.clip(..., 0.05, 0.95)`; at confounding=2.0 the true e(x) falls outside that range for about 14% of units, so even the correctly specified logistic model is biased there. The outcome model (`Z = [1, X]`, linear ridge on random Fourier features) is misspecified, because E[cos(wY/h+b)|X] is nonlinear in X. That leaves a nonzero mean in g under H0. A deep kernel fitted to the train half to maximise d/σ could learn to amplify this systematic bias, which would raise both power and type-I. With R_NULL=3 this cannot be detected.

The alternative is only an additive mean shift in pixel space (`delta * T * v`), drawn from the same image distribution in both arms. This is much simpler than the paper's structured image/text/graph alternatives. A learned linear-like projection is enough to win, so the result says little about 'structured outcomes' as such.

Only the binary contrast do(A=1) vs do(A=0) is tested, where `w = T/e - (1-T)/(1-e)`. The paper's general soft interventions π, π' are a special case not covered, and everything uses random-Fourier-feature approximations (D_F=64) instead of exact kernels.

Deep-kernel training is short and unselected: 60 full-batch Adam steps, a fixed lr of 0.02, no restarts, and no train-half validation or early stopping. The `_crit` objective is evaluated with nuisances (`_fit_B`, `etr`) fitted in-sample on the same train data used for training, so the training criterion is optimistically biased. Held-out evaluation itself is clean.

The sign-flip calibration assumes each pseudo-feature g_i is symmetric about zero under H0. With DR weights and clipped propensities it is only mean-zero, approximately. The test is also one-sided (`null >= obs`). This is acceptable for the cross-U statistic but only approximately valid.
summary: The lab does test the paper's core idea in miniature. It builds a doubly robust pseudo-embedding of the treatment effect from cross-fitted propensity and outcome-embedding models, trains a deep kernel (an MLP plus a characteristic component) to maximise a studentised cross-U power criterion on the train half, and runs a sign-flip test on the held-out half. It compares against a median-bandwidth kernel and a 5-point bandwidth grid optimised on the same criterion. For a given seed, the data, random Fourier feature weights and sign-flip draws are seeded independently of the method, so all arms see identical inputs. The baselines are not sabotaged. Fidelity is medium for four reasons: the alternative is a simple mean shift on 8x8 digits, only a binary treatment contrast is tested, kernels are approximated with random Fourier features, and kernel training is minimal. The main weaknesses are (a) type-I error is estimated from just 3 null replications, so the 'well-calibrated' half of the claim is effectively unchecked; (b) power from 6 replications has resolution far coarser than the declared minimum effect; and (c) clipped propensities combined with a misspecified linear outcome model can leave bias under the null, which a power-trained deep kernel might exploit.
